📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

State law caps what you can charge as a notary for each notarization, at $10 or less in most states, so notarizing alone pays little. To earn more, charge travel fees for mobile appointments and qualify as a loan signing agent, since a loan signing typically pays $50 to $200.

A routine notarization takes 5 to 10 minutes, and its fee can’t exceed $2 per signer under New York law or $10 per act under Florida law.

No state caps a signing agent’s fee, because the job is more than a notarization. Lenders, title companies, and signing services hire you as a contractor to print the loan documents, meet the borrowers, notarize their signatures, and send the package back. The National Notary Association says the signing itself takes 45 minutes to a few hours, not counting travel.

Work up to signings in this order:.

At a signing, send every question about the loan’s terms to the loan officer, since a notary who isn’t a lawyer can’t give legal advice.

Fees for notarizing are taxable income, but the IRS’s Schedule SE instructions leave them out of self-employment tax, the Social Security and Medicare tax on work you do for yourself. That exemption covers the notarizations alone, so travel fees and the rest of a signing fee count as self-employment income. Record each signing’s notarization fees apart from the rest of its pay, and set aside part of every payment for tax.

It has been revealed that lifeline takes up to $9.25 a month off one phone or home internet blueprint if your household’s income is low or anyone in it gets SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal housing assistance, or a veterans pension. Apply through the National Verifier, Lifeline’s application site, then pick a company whose plan costs little or nothing after the discount.

Only about 8 million of the nearly 38 million households that qualify have signed up, according to USAC, the nonprofit that runs Lifeline for the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

You qualify if your household’s income is no more than 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, a limit that Lifeline’s income table shows in dollars by household size. You also qualify if anyone in your household gets SNAP, Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), federal housing assistance such as a Section 8 voucher, or the Veterans Pension and Survivors Benefit. A February 2026 FCC proposal would limit Lifeline to U.S. citizens and certain legal immigrants and could require a full Social Security number, but it isn’t final.

Sources indicate that each household, meaning everyone at one address who shares income and expenses, gets one discount, so a parent on SSI who lives alone can get their own. On qualifying Tribal lands, the discount is up to $34.25 a month.

According to recent reports, apply online through the National Verifier, by mail with a paper application, or with help from a phone or internet manufacturer that takes Lifeline. Oregon and Texas residents apply through their state’s Lifeline program instead.

Industry observers note that then use the Companies Near Me tool to find the companies serving your ZIP code, and compare what each charges after the discount, since some Lifeline phone plans cost nothing. Choose a plan with data, because phone service alone gets only up to $5.25. A retiree on SSI who puts the $9.25 toward a $15 prepaid plan with talk, text, and data pays $5.75 a month before taxes.

In a recent development, on a free proposal, use the service at least once every 30 days, or the organization can cut it off after a 15-day warning. Lifeline rechecks your eligibility every year, and a recertification notice left unanswered for 60 days ends the discount. Other programs offer emergency help with rent, utilities, and food.

Before you apply, gather a benefit letter issued in the past 12 months, a screenshot of your benefits portal, or last year’s tax return, since Lifeline can ask for proof.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

It has been revealed that true Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

In a recent development, the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

In a recent development, another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

Recent findings suggest that the cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive proposal for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Sources indicate that financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable proposal to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

In a recent development, moneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

According to recent reports, moneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a blueprint that fit my unique situation and goals.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured strategy to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

In a recent development, ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Sources indicate that regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Get two or three itemized bids on the same finished proposal, then set your renovation budget at the bid you pick plus 10% to 20% for hidden problems like rot or old wiring. To stay under it, make every choice before demolition, get each change priced in writing, and pay from savings where you can.

Of the homeowners who renovated in 2025, 37% went over budget, the 2026 U.S. Houzz & Home Study found. More than half of them blamed products or services that cost more than they expected, and 35% had picked pricier materials than they first planned.

In a recent development, A budget built from a finished, priced strategy makes both causes less likely. The bid prices what you’ll actually build, and the extra 10% to 20% is there for what nobody can see until the walls are open.

Build the budget in this order:.

Recent findings suggest that say a couple’s chosen bid for a bathroom remodel is $18,000. They set the budget at $21,000, a $3,000 cushion, and when the crew finds rotted subfloor that adds $1,900, they finish $1,100 under budget without borrowing. Cash saved ahead in a high-yield savings account is the cheapest way to pay, since a personal loan or a loan against your home’s equity adds interest.

Industry observers note that then keep the initiative from changing. Before demolition, choose every fixture and material, so you never pick in a hurry once the walls are open. Put each change in writing with its price before the crew starts it, and compare your spending with the plan every week.

Keep the cushion for hidden problems like that rotted subfloor, and pay for any upgrade you want midway by cutting a nice-to-have.

Helpusadopt.org, for one, applies each grant to an adoption’s final fees and won’t reimburse fees you’ve already paid, even with a card or loan. Charge the last $10,000 to a card, and a $10,000 grant has nothing left to cover.

Start with these five nonprofits, the first two open to families of any faith, marital status, or sexual orientation:.

Sources indicate that helpusadopt.org, Show Hope, and Lifesong all need your application before your child moves in. Apply to several at once, since Helpusadopt.org still considers families who have won another grant.

Recent findings suggest that keep saving and fundraising while you wait, since Gift of Adoption looks for families who have saved and raised what they can. Raise money through a nonprofit’s page, such as Lifesong’s, rather than GoFundMe, so donors get a receipt. Then borrow only what’s left, on a monthly payment you’ve budgeted for.

Say a $5,000 grant and a $7,000 interest-free loan cover a $12,000 gap, and you repay the loan over four years. That’s $146 a month, $7,000 in all. Put all $12,000 on a card at 22% instead, near the average the Federal Reserve reports for cards that charge interest. Paying it off over the same four years takes $378 a month, about $18,150 in all.

Before your home study is approved, gather your latest tax return, two months of pay stubs, and a list of your assets and debts, and line up two references. Then your first applications can go out the week the approval arrives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most key things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who at the moment draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

It has been revealed that those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

According to recent reports, but when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

Industry observers note that that little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

Industry observers note that in between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

Recent findings suggest that when you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

According to recent reports, at that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be substantial enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re new to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

According to recent reports, shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

In a recent development, but wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:.

According to recent reports, whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result! Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

In a recent development, to really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

In a recent development, by the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:.

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:.

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

Sources indicate that the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a significant boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

It has been revealed that first of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Sources indicate that now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all challenges. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions.

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35. Look at the difference in their benefits:.

It has been revealed that so the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the major earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if your job-based or marketplace health plan covers emergency care, the No Surprises Act bars an ER and its doctors from billing you more than your in-network copay, coinsurance, and deductible, even when they’re out of network. Compare any ER bill with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, pay what it says you owe, and dispute the rest.

Industry observers note that say you have an emergency appendectomy at an in-network hospital, the surgeon is out of network, and your initiative’s in-network coinsurance for the surgery comes to $250. If the surgeon then bills you $3,200, you still owe only the $250.

The No Surprises Act, in force since January 1, 2022, limits what you owe to that in-network share for care your strategy covers in three situations:.

The law leaves out ground ambulances, which can still charge out-of-network rates unless your state forbids it. You can give up the protection by signing a notice-and-consent form, a waiver that lets the provider bill you more than your in-network share. No provider may ask you to sign one for emergency care before you’re stable, and anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists, and assistant surgeons may never ask.

Sources indicate that to spot a violation, compare the bill with your explanation of benefits, the statement your insurer sends after it processes a claim. The amount it claims you owe should match the bill.

Recent findings suggest that call the provider’s billing office about any charge above that amount, cite the No Surprises Act, and ask it to cut the bill or refund what you overpaid. If it won’t, file a complaint with the No Surprises Help Desk online or at 1-800-985-3059, seven days a week, and the Help Desk can refer it to a state regulator.

While the complaint is open, pay the amount your explanation of benefits indicates you owe, and nothing above it.

Buying From a Private Seller? Try a Private-Party Auto Loan Before a Personal Loan

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for a used car from a private seller, ask a credit union or your bank for a private-party auto loan.
  • Recent findings suggest that A seller you found on Facebook Marketplace or through a friend won’t arrange financing the way a dealer would.
  • Sources indicate that an auto lender can charge less than a personal lender because the car is collateral, which it can repossess if you stop paying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for a used car from a private seller, ask a credit union or your bank for a private-party auto loan. The car secures it, so it usually costs less than a personal loan, and the lender can pay off any loan the seller still owes. Save the personal loan for a car too old or cheap to qualify.

Recent findings suggest that A seller you found on Facebook Marketplace or through a friend won’t arrange financing the way a dealer would. The loan is yours to line up, and the kind you choose changes the rate you pay.

Sources indicate that an auto lender can charge less than a personal lender because the car is collateral, which it can repossess if you stop paying. Say you borrow $10,000 of a $14,000 price over five years, at 8% on an auto loan or 11% on a personal loan. The auto loan runs about $203 a month and the personal loan about $217, so the auto loan costs about $880 less in total.

According to recent reports, before you shop, find a lender that makes private-party loans, since not all do. Bank of America, for one, finances only dealer purchases. Then get pre-approved, so you know your rate and how much you can spend, and check the lender’s limits. Many lenders cap the car’s age and mileage and set a minimum loan, so a high-mileage older car or a loan of a couple of thousand dollars may not qualify.

According to recent reports, once you’ve chosen the car, the lender will want a copy of the title and a bill of sale, plus a payoff quote from the seller’s lender if the seller still owes on the car. Have your lender pay the seller’s lender directly and write the seller a check for the rest, so that loan is cleared before the title is signed over to you.

Sources indicate that A personal loan is the better tool when the car falls outside those limits, the seller won’t wait for that paperwork, or you’d rather not have a lender listed on the title until the loan is paid. Either way, pay an independent mechanic to inspect the car, and check its title history with a report from a provider the Justice Department lists at vehiclehistory.gov.

Meet the seller at your bank or credit union to close the sale, so the money changes hands only when the title does.

#79457. The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s.
  • Industry observers note that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival.
  • We're not in an official bear market, yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

Industry observers note that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

So I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

Sources indicate that as the midterm elections revealed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

According to recent reports, as long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

Sources indicate that but that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

Sources indicate that when the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The new car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

If you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

According to recent reports, if you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering significant losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

Retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

Recent findings suggest that how do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

According to recent reports, so how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

In a recent development, according to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market shows up about once every six years.

In other words, if you initiative on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

Hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Recent findings suggest that bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Sources indicate that two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

Industry observers note that but here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

It has been revealed that hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

In a recent development, my takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, initiative on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

Industry observers note that during a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

During a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, new socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

With this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Industry observers note that therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

According to recent reports, 2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

Industry observers note that 3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

Recent findings suggest that 4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

In a recent development, 5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

Sources indicate that 6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

It has been revealed that you can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

Sources indicate that the market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

It has been revealed that if your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your strategy has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Sources indicate that compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

Sources indicate that so go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

It has been revealed that are you finding it more comforting to be retired during a downturn, or more stressful? How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

Industry observers note that if you want a roadmap for getting through downturns and coming out richer, pick up a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller. It covers how to keep investing when everybody else is scared, so you can reach financial independence sooner.

  • Most of those forms don’t have to go out until January 31, and a few not until mid-February, so a return filed in January can reach the IRS before they reach you.
  • The IRS checks each return against the copies it received, and income missing from yours can bring a CP2000 notice proposing the tax on it, plus interest from the April due date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you file your tax return, wait until every W-2, 1099, 1098, and 1095-A due to you has arrived, which can take until mid-February. The IRS gets a copy of each form, and when your return leaves one out, it can send a notice proposing more tax, plus interest.

Most of those forms don’t have to go out until January 31, and a few not until mid-February, so a return filed in January can reach the IRS before they reach you.

The IRS checks each return against the copies it received, and income missing from yours can bring a CP2000 notice proposing the tax on it, plus interest from the April due date.

Recent findings suggest that say you’re in the 22% tax bracket and file on January 25. A week later, a Form 1099-INT arrives showing $600 of interest from your high-yield savings account. At 22%, that’s $132 of tax your return left out. Unless you amend your return first, expect a CP2000 for that $132, plus interest.

These must go out by January 31:.

If one of these hasn’t arrived by mid-February, ask the sender for a copy, and ask for a corrected copy of any that’s wrong. When a missing form won’t come in time to file, report the income from your own statements, since the IRS requires you to report interest even when no 1099-INT arrives.

The IRS gives brokers until mid-February to send consolidated 1099s, which combine investment sales, dividends, and interest. HealthCare.gov notes Form 1095-A, for Marketplace health coverage, should reach you by then, and not to file until you have an accurate one. If you have a brokerage account that isn’t an IRA, wait until mid-March. Companies and funds sometimes change how a dividend they already reported is taxed, which means a corrected 1099, and Ally says those changes most likely come before March 15.

Build a checklist of forms from last year’s return, then add one for each new job, account, and loan.

Sources indicate that so write the list before you shop a single sale. Put down each item you need, the most you’ll pay for it, and a total for everything you strategy to buy through Cyber Monday, so even a run of real deals stays inside your budget.

This is how a fixed budget covers more of your list, since every item bought at its low leaves more money for the ones you haven’t bought yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deposit a money order at your own bank or credit union, or cash a postal money order at any post office, and you won’t pay a fee. When you sell something, ask for a postal money order and confirm it with USPS before the buyer leaves, since you’ll repay your bank for any fake that bounces.

Anywhere else, cashing one can cost you. Each check casher sets its own rules and may charge a fee, MoneyGram says, and Western Union notes that not all of its locations can cash one, even the store that sold it.

It has been revealed that so the company that issued yours decides where it’s free. The U.S. Postal Service cashes its own money orders free at any post office and lets anyone holding one confirm it’s real. Western Union and MoneyGram send you to a bank or a check casher, so deposit theirs at your own bank or credit union. Without a bank account, a postal money order is the only kind you can count on cashing for free.

According to recent reports, say a buyer pays $400 for your couch with a postal money order. Before the couch leaves, hold the money order up to a light. A watermark and a thread running top to bottom with the letters USPS should show through, the amount in words should match the numbers, and a domestic one can’t be for more than $1,000. Then confirm it on USPS’s money order status page, using its serial number, post office number, and amount, or by calling 1-866-459-7822.

In a recent development, at your bank, read the app’s list of accepted items before you snap photos. Some apps refuse money orders, and Wells Fargo’s turns away postal ones, so hand a refused one to a teller. At a post office, bring a photo ID and sign the money order only at the counter, in front of the clerk, as USPS directs. Either way, photograph both sides first to keep a record of its serial number.

Recent findings suggest that don’t treat money showing in your account as proof the money order was real. By law, banks have to make deposits available rapidly, the Federal Trade Commission notes, while catching a fake can take weeks.

#79453. Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1445 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m a proponent of stealth wealth.
  • Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades.
  • Recent findings suggest that so by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend.

Recent findings suggest that so by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

Sources indicate that in private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better. Here are three simple steps to follow:.

1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

Industry observers note that 2) Drive an old car. Driving a latest car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

In a recent development, once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

My parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

Sources indicate that at the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 31-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

Then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

According to recent reports, and you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

According to recent reports, today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I stopped needing respect from everyone.

Industry observers note that I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such conspicuous spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? We think to ourselves. But we’re missing something important.

Recent findings suggest that her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

This resonated with me as a minority who came to America for high school and faced various racist incidents. Racism is one of the deepest forms of disrespect because you're insulted just for being who you are. Respect, especially for elders, is a major part of Asian culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

When you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

At 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

According to recent reports, then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

Today, insults from random folks feel more like pinches instead of body blows. The passive income is doing its job as a shield.

As a dad now, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no big deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

Sources indicate that in that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the substantial deal?

Yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

Industry observers note that reaching FIRE doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect.

Maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

Whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else. Know that there is an incredible joy of being a nobody so long as you have your finances in order.

For many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

Sources indicate that that’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

Readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

It has been revealed that stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

Sources indicate that people spend thousands on designer clothes to impress strangers. A free expert review of your finances is a far better flex, even if nobody sees it.

Sources indicate that before you pay to haul away something that won’t sell, offer it in your town’s Freecycle group, where neighbors pick up usable things for free. Joining costs nothing. Post a wanted request there before you buy, since a neighbor may already have one to give.

Sources indicate that A working treadmill that nobody will buy still costs money to get rid of. LoadUp, a national junk-removal service, lists treadmill pickup from $150.

On Freecycle, a neighbor who wants it can haul it away for nothing. The Freecycle Network is a nonprofit that counts over 12 million members, and volunteer moderators run its more than 5,000 local town groups. Members post offers of things they’re done with and wanted requests for things they need.

Freecycle’s guidelines require every post to be free and rule out swaps and trading, so something too dated or worn to sell can still go to someone who needs it.

Sources indicate that to give, join your town’s group and post an offer with up to three photos and a description of the item’s condition and how pickup works. Keep your address and phone number out of the post. Freecycle suggests waiting for a handful of replies, or overnight, then picking one person rather than leaving the item out for whoever arrives first. Agree on a time with that person and leave the item on your porch or in the garage, which keeps strangers out of your house. If you’d rather drop things off than arrange a pickup, look for a town swap shop or free store.

According to recent reports, to get things, post a wanted request for the specific item you’d otherwise buy, such as a bookcase for a 30-inch wall. Freecycle’s guidelines also ask members to use wanted posts sparingly, and the limit on them varies by group. A neighborhood Buy Nothing group, another kind of local giveaway group, takes the same request. Answer an offer you want right away with a pickup time, then arrive when you said you would. Collect the item from a porch or a public place, and bring someone along for any pickup inside a home.

Join your town’s group a week before a cleanout, since some groups approve new members first and a post can wait for a volunteer moderator to check it.
