Industry News: Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu.
  • Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.
  • It has been revealed that “Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

It has been revealed that “Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”.

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

In a recent development, the recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

Industry observers note that the fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Sources indicate that satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung stated he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that on Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:.

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

It has been revealed that the route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#79379. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife.
  • According to recent reports, as expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts.
  • Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

According to recent reports, as expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Recent findings suggest that in Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

Recent findings suggest that the people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Sources indicate that early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

According to recent reports, habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Industry observers note that A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

In a recent development, farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Industry observers note that saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In a recent development, leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Sources indicate that another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

According to recent reports, locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

It has been revealed that elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India.

It has been revealed that in Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Manufacturer.

Industry observers note that none of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Tech giant officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

#79375. Breaking: Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (696 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu.
  • According to recent reports, as soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

According to recent reports, as soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

Recent findings suggest that “Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

The ridge on ChekiGo. Photo: Eric Bazon.

Industry observers note that since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

Sources indicate that the climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon.

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It has been revealed that it took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below reveals that the fresh French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”.

It has been revealed that but this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni.

#79372. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (609 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island.
  • In a recent development, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital.
  • The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

In a recent development, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

In a recent development, with no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

In a recent development, the paddling portion went rapidly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”.

Using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they noted.

Sources indicate that mcDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Sources indicate that slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

Industry observers note that “One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We swiftly packed our boats and got on the water.”.

Recent findings suggest that in Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”.

#79371. Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2884 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail.
  • By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while.
  • The views this morning were unbelievable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail. I was really hoping that we were going to get surprised last night by Leaf at some point, but she never did wind up catching up to us. At least today she’ll be heading into town from a trailhead less than 20 miles from where we were camped. So, she isn’t too far from a road, a town, and some hiking friends. I made coffee this morning pretty early and then laid in my tent for a while. Then the two of us got packed up and were walking on the trail before the sun was up. There isn’t too much awaiting us along the trail up ahead. Today we will be going past that major trailhead and highway crossing about 19 miles into the day. But other than that, it is just going to be us and the trail for the next few days. Depending on how far we go today and tomorrow, we’ll hopefully be able to head into town the following evening to resupply and recharge.

A small bear track in the muddy red clay.

By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while. And the trail actually had some fun surprises for us. Thanks to all of the rain, the trail had been covered in mud for the last couple of days. Which meant that any animal that hiked through the area would leave deep footprints in the trail. We got to follow the path of a bear which had been walking through this area in the last couple of days. It left behind such clear footprints in the red clay mud. It was cool to see the larger prints left behind by its back feet. This section of the trail was beautiful all on its own, but the prints in the mud added something special to it all.

The views this morning were unbelievable. After all of the rain the red clay has the most incredible, deep color to it. And all of the trees and plants are vibrant and lush.

For the first hour or two of the day the trail was a dark red clay, complimented quite well by the lush pine trees and other shrubs surrounding the trail. The rising sun lit up the rocky mountainside off in the distance and made the red clay glow. That was a stunning way to start off the morning. We had some gradual climbing to do and continued to see bear prints along the trail on and off. If I was a bear, I would also love to follow the trail. It is a perfect path through the wilderness! It’s also one reason why some hikers prefer to set up their camp a little way off the trail at night. In the night, the trail is an animal highway through the woods. You never know what you’ll see if you follow a trail through the dark.

I liked the way that the layer of clouds off in the distance was resting right above the mountain range. The Arizona Trail sure had a lot of trees today!

Lucky for us, the mud wasn’t too bad this morning. Most of the moisture had been sucked in to the earth already. Leaving behind only the deep, saturated color that the water left behind. These sections of red clay are some of my favorites here in Arizona. The color looks incredible right beside the deep greens that we are able to enjoy thanks to all of the rain. I’ve had a lot of people reach out to say that the red clay typically doesn’t look nearly as vibrant as it does right now. All of the rain makes the color all the deeper, which I’m quite thankful for.

One particular stretch of trail that walked along a large red rock hillside.

It has been revealed that over the course of the morning the trail was following along a large cluster of rocks off in the distance. Some of them were shaped like tall, jagged chimneys. I really enjoyed the view as we got even closer to the rocks, before eventually the trail veered off. We actually ran into some people on the trail today as well. There are a ton of road crossings and trailhead throughout this area. One guy was out doing some trail maintenance scouting. I’m sure that the individuals doing trail maintenance through this area have their work cut out for them with all of the rain and flash flooding. An entire section of trail can so easily get washed away if enough water pours through an area. We’ve been lucky so far with the state of the trail. But there have definitely been a lot of sections and areas with fresh rock fall.

According to recent reports, clouds starting to roll in off in the distance. I thought we were going to get poured on! But as we stood on top of a ridge, we could see the storm blowing off and away from us.

Recent findings suggest that by the late morning the temperature dropped a bit, and some dark clouds began to roll in. I hadn’t seen any rain in the forecast, but it certainly seemed like we had some coming for us. We stopped on top of a hill for a quick break, and each put our rain gear on while we watched it pour down off in the distance. It made me think about Leaf behind us, and all of our friends up ahead of us. The storm managed to skirt right on by us, and it hardly rained more than a sprinkle. But we could tell that someone somewhere was getting rained on. It felt nice to keep the rain gear on as we continued along, at least for a little while. We watched as the bulk of the storm blew by us and the skies got bright and blue off in the distance up ahead.

It has been revealed that for a mile or two the trail slowly approached this cluster of unique rocks. A couple of them look like stone pillars.

As we got closer to the trailhead and highway crossing, we did wind up getting rained on a bit. Which was surprising because the rain started just as the skies turned blue! It was only a sprinkle though. I used my sun umbrella to stay dry and the rain passed promptly. Though, even just a light rain caused the mud on the trail to build back up again. I’m just hoping that the mud won’t be too bad for the rest of the day. Prior to reaching the trailhead, we ran into a couple more day hikers and one person on horseback with another horse being pulled behind them. The second horse had the cutest little pink saddle on. Then it wasn’t long until we reached the trailhead as well.

These bright yellow wildflowers have been growing all along the trail.

Arizona Trail signs near the trailhead about 20 miles into our day.

Sources indicate that for some reason it always feels exciting to pass by a trailhead, even if you aren’t heading into town. Perhaps it’s the possibility of receiving some trail magic there or having something else eventful occur. When we actually passed by the trailhead though there was hardly anyone around and we just continued along. And we only made it another mile or two before we encountered the next obstacle ahead of us. There was another deep river crossing for us to ford! This one was quite easy in comparison to our river crossing yesterday. We walked around to see if there was any way that we could avoid getting our feet wet, but there was not. So, we both plunged in and got our shoes and socks soaked. Then sat on the other side of the river to enjoy a lunch break.

After Slide and I crossed the river, we sat here in the grass to eat lunch.

The sky was still dark off in the distance and it certainly felt like it was going to rain at some point. Both of us figured this would be a good time to stop and eat, just in case the rain did start up. I had packed out one of those tasty bite tikka masala meals which I enjoyed there. Those always do a great job of filling me up. Then I cleaned out my socks and shoes and debated on whether or not I should put my rain gear back on. We were going to begin going uphill, so I knew I was going to get super-hot in rain gear. But if it’s windy at all then I still get wet when I’m using just my umbrella. I decided to opt against it and just figured that if the rain did start and was heavy, I could just stop and put my rain jacket on later.

In the early evening the trail briefly followed along this massive slab of rock. It reminded me of sections of the Appalachian Trail in New York.

The rain wound up holding off as we continued along. It sprinkled on us briefly but didn’t persist. Once we left the river, we did have a bit of climbing to do. Then we were up on top of the nearby hill and just continued along up there. In some places the trail itself was just a massive boulder beneath the ground. We had some open and exposed views, and the weather was nice and cool. It felt like we had gotten pretty lucky already for the day. It wouldn’t be long before I had to get my feet wet again in yet another small stream crossing. I probably could have tried harder and kept my feet dry, but it felt like a lot of work. I also always have the strong memory in my mind of slipping on a rock in a river crossing in Northern California on the PCT and breaking 2 of my fingers last year. All to avoid getting my feet wet! I actually wound up getting more wet than I would have if I just crossed through the river normally, because I slipped and fell. Of course, at the time I didn’t realize that I’d broken 2 of my fingers. But 4 months later I still couldn’t apply any pressure to the two fingers on my right hand, so it feels like a safe assumption now.

Recent findings suggest that A photo that Slide took of me when we were on top of this ridge. The trail stayed up there for the rest of the evening and the views just got better and better.

Sources indicate that as we continued along the trail was pretty rocky, but in exchange we were graced with some great views. The trail went through some areas with vibrant foliage as well. The leaves were a perfect spectrum of light greens, yellows, oranges, and deep reds. It reminds me so much of hiking in Colorado this time of year. We even saw a bunch more bear prints along the trail over the course of the evening. And some prints that appeared to be a large dog. They definitely didn’t look like mountain lion prints, in my opinion. I’m not sure what else they could be besides a dog!

I figured these were just big dog prints, but I still like the way that they looked in the mud.

By the time that the sun began to set we were up top of a ridge and would be continuing along it for the rest of the evening. The sun cast an incredible glow across the wheat grass and other plants surrounding the trail. There were loads of bright yellow wildflowers and prickly pear cacti throughout the area as well. It was a really beautiful way to end off the day. Sometime after 5PM we passed my favorite bear prints of the entire day. There were some prints which were incredibly deep and had standing water inside of them. It just really highlighted how massive the prints were. I wonder where this bear was going, and if it was the same bear whose prints we saw earlier on in the day. I’m sure it’s not, but bears can travel very far in a day if they want to.

Perfectly defined bear prints right on the trail.

In a recent development, in the early evening, we entered into the Mazatzal Wilderness in the Tonto National Forest. At this point the sun was just starting to go down, and the sky was putting on quite the show for us. The trail got much rockier in this section and there were way more cacti lining the trail as well. The timing wasn’t great, because we would be looking for camping sometime soon. When the trail is lined in rocks and cacti it can be hard to find a place to set up your tent. As we walked, I snacked on some pistachios and enjoyed the views. We were in the perfect place to be able to enjoy the sunset this evening.

The sun was beginning to set, and we were in the perfect place to enjoy it.

In a recent development, the trail stayed pretty much the same for the rest of the night. There were rocks all over the place and a ton of cacti. Camping options seemed limited at best, if not nonexistent. But we just kept our eyes peeled for any area with less rocks and some flat ground. Just after it got dark, we did wind up finding an area just off the trail which didn’t seem too bad. It was a little rocky and lumpy but was definitely much better than what we had been seeing. It was hard to imagine that we would find anything much better than this anytime soon. So, we decided to just call it a day then and there. We both got our tents set up, and it was a great feeling to take off my shoes and socks. They weren’t soaked, but they definitely weren’t dry. The worst part about wet shoes and socks, in opinion, is putting them back on the next morning. Especially when it is cold out! It could take my breath away.

Enjoying that last bit of light before the sun completely dipped behind the mountains off in the distance.

Sources indicate that once my tent was up, I got comfortable inside and ate something. Then did my stretching routine before calling it a night. We made it 31 miles today which was pretty good. Sure, we could have gone a bit further to make our life easier tomorrow and the next day. But we certainly didn’t need to. I think we’ll wind up having another early start tomorrow morning which will make up for it. There is a ton of elevation gain tomorrow, so I’m curious to see how that goes.

It has been revealed that if you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The tall wheatgrass looked almost pink under the glow of those cotton candy clouds.

Sources indicate that this was easily one of the best views that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying thus far on the Arizona Trail. The sunsets and sunrises out here have been fantastic.

Breaking: Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long newly introduced route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • It has been revealed that this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long newly introduced route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

It has been revealed that this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to rapidly find a different goal.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us latest hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

It has been revealed that steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

Sources indicate that chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” mentioned Steadman.

It has been revealed that “We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

Industry observers note that “The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Sources indicate that summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, “The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

Industry observers note that after some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

In a recent development, [We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

In a recent development, happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

Sources indicate that “It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • Sources indicate that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • Sources indicate that it was a very hard life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

Sources indicate that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

Sources indicate that it was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

Recent findings suggest that the small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill claims, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

It has been revealed that the spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that macAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (365 w)

Tech Report: Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (365 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • Sources indicate that kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Sources indicate that kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Sources indicate that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His prepares expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Sources indicate that edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

In a recent development, A cross-country walking journey, Edwards notes, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

Latest Update: Adventure Links of the Week

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web.
  • Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock.
  • A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Industry observers note that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in Fresh York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

Industry observers note that this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

Sources indicate that A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage indicates her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

Industry observers note that we Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

According to recent reports, this comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#79354. Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1318 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.
  • There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.
  • In a recent development, I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.

There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.

In a recent development, I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear. Maybe they’re worried that the things I normally handle will now fall into their laps. Then there are the people who sound surprised or curious. I may have to explain exactly what backpacking is and what thru-hiking entails. Those conversations lead to a whole different brand of questions. These are the best discussions, and I can go down all kinds of rabbit holes about gear, food, concerns about animals, and where I’m going to sleep.

The question, though, is still this: Why am I going to hike for six months, leaving a perfectly good couch, bed, wife, career, and a couple of affectionate cats behind? All to be cold, wet, and worn out most days from doing nothing but walking? Miles and miles of walking.

I have to go way back, maybe 14 years ago, when my wife and I were exposing the kids to all kinds of different vacations, ideally the kind that didn’t cost much. For several years, we had been camping at National Parks, enjoying the sights and activities. One of those years, when we were in the Rockies, we saw a young couple leaving camp with their tiny kids, each carrying an even tinier backpack. We remembered a couple of backpacking trips we’d taken after we got married but before we had kids. The gear had been sitting on a shelf for years, but at least we still had some.

“Let’s take the kids next year!”.

It has been revealed that the next year, we suited up. Our kids now had their own tiny packs. We had food, fuel, and ponchos in case it rained.

Did I mention we were on a small section of the Appalachian Trail in the Smoky Mountains?

In a recent development, it rained for three days straight before we even started our hike, and then it rained for the three days we were on the trail. Thankfully, we stayed in shelters, but there were a lot of lessons learned. Lessons about food, clothing, footwear, water treatment and yes, raingear. Still, I came off the trail with a huge smile. Can’t say that about the kids, but for me, I had a blast! Spoiler – both my kids are now young adults and camp, sometimes willingly but I’m getting distracted.

The biggest lesson for me came when we got off the trail. My daughter pointed to the large sign behind me that mentioned “Appalachian Trail” which told me about its more than 2,150 miles of hiking that people tackle every year.

Industry observers note that pretty sure my response was, “That’s ridiculous. No one can do that.” The food, if nothing else, would weigh hundreds of pounds, not to mention all the fuel we’d need to boil water. It would take an Ironman-caliber person just to carry all of that.

It has been revealed that somewhere around there, I started going down the rabbit hole of research. Resupply every few days? Okay. That’s feasible. Water filters? That would save a lot of time compared to hours of boiling water (which, yes, we had been doing). Lighter-weight gear? I could do that.

I fell in love with the concept of it.

Sources indicate that so why? Why would I spent 6 months in the woods hiking?

It wasn’t the romantic feel of trail life (though a lot of trail journals do talk very positively about it). I could talk about my love of nature and wanting to be out in the woods, watching the slow change of the seasons. That isn’t completely it. I can do that from my bedroom window. I could mention making fresh friends or reducing the clutter in my life. I could learn that last lesson by just going to my parents’ house and looking at the hoarding nightmare in their basement that’s slowly becoming my problem. All important things and outcomes I’ve read about from other hikers.

No, I think for me, I fell in love with the idea of an adventure. One that would be within my grasp as a middle-aged, desk-jockey engineer who really needed some outdoor time to recharge his batteries before returning to the world of engineering work. Not quite ready for retirement, but not wanting to spend all my years letting my glutes go to crap while I sit in a chair and pound on a keyboard, arguing over engineering details with team members spread out across the globe while we work toward a common, upcoming design.

It has been revealed that I don’t picture it as some grand adventure of heading off at sunrise, marching to Mordor with a ring, or even trekking through the wilderness to find myself. But I do want to have an adventure that, as I get older, I can fondly stare off into space remembering… remembering the tough days, the worn-out feelings, the beautiful views, the green tunnel, new friendships, and new experiences.

According to recent reports, that’s why I’m heading out to the woods for six months. It’s not to run away from legal trouble (I don’t even have any overdue parking tickets). It’s not to flee from my job (I actually do like what I’m doing, but after thirty-plus years, a break would be nice). It’s not to escape from my family (I happen to like them, too. Well, most of the time, but I’m sure that feeling is mutual).

So, if I had to state the biggest, single reason, it’s because I’m looking to have an adventure, one where the journey is the destination. And if I can make it to Katahdin with a bunch of new friends and great stories, all the better.

It has been revealed that this website contains affiliate links, which means The Trek may receive a percentage of any product or service you purchase using the links in the articles or advertisements. The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

About me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Major Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole fresh world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

Good luck on your AT adventure and I look forward to your posts!

#79351. Industry News: Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • According to recent reports, hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • In a recent development, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their plans to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

According to recent reports, hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

In a recent development, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding tech giant Ousland Colliard.

Sources indicate that indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

According to recent reports, satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

It has been revealed that american Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

In a recent development, another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Recent findings suggest that max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Industry observers note that satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 strategy is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

Industry observers note that if successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

According to recent reports, last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

Recent findings suggest that A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Industry observers note that gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and proposal to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

In a recent development, the Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a latest route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

According to recent reports, their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team looks a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

Industry observers note that the wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#79348. Breaking: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (645 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” noted Baia.

In a recent development, he indicates the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

According to recent reports, in addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

Recent findings suggest that after their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick fresh layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

“Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

Industry observers note that they were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

In a recent development, “Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Revealed

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In a recent development, in addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

Sources indicate that the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

Recent findings suggest that for best feature film, the competition unveiled Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Industry observers note that director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” stated Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.
