#79342. Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2383 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I apologize in advance for the ending to this post.
  • With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m.
  • With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  49,771 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:30.

I apologize in advance for the ending to this post. After some deliberation, I have decided to break the narrative of my last day on the John Muir Trail into two. This narrative will cover the last day up to about one or two miles from the terminus at Happy Isles. The next shall cover that ending as well as my departure from Yosemite. The reason for this you will understand when you read about the very unfortunate incident that occurred just as I reached the end of my hike.

With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m. and knew I would not go back to sleep. I had risen to pee several times in the night, and each time I was filled with awe to see the silent sentinels of granite towering all around me in the starlight. With the glimmer of dawn, it was even better.

With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.

Despite the weather report, it was not as cold as the night before, and there was no sign of frost on the ground. I believe the temperature hovered just above freezing.

It has been revealed that I wanted to start especially early today because I was catching the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) bus to Merced where son Gabriel was to pick me up. I thought there was a 4:30 bus that got to Merced at about 8:30 and I figured we could be back in Santa Rosa by midnight if we made that schedule. There were earlier and later departures (up to 7:00 p.m.) but that seemed the most reasonable to aim for with a fast pace.

So, I did my morning chores and ablutions, including breaking down my tent, with its broken pole. (The repair had held solidly all night.).

The shear on the broken pole was mild enough the repair was successful.

As I did so, I watched the morning sunlight gradually fill the space between the mountains and start to land on their upper ridges.

This spot was just such a glorious location.

I understood why I was I alone up there. The site had no water and was not even within a mile of a water source. The night before I needed water to soak my dinner. This morning I needed water to soak my breakfast, and to fill my bidet. That’s a lot of water needed before we even consider basic hydration. Even with all that, the location on this high little mesa of rock, with such fantastic views in all directions, made the water risk totally worth it.

As I started down, I realized my elevation profile for the day included 6,660 feet of descent to the valley floor, with only a bit over 700 feet of ascent. Right away I knocked out a few of those 700 feet as the trail started by climbing a small hill.

Cresting the hill, I started down, encountering a group of older hikers coming up. They spent the night at Sunrise High Sierra Camp and were day-hiking from there. They asked me where I started from and were duly impressed when I replied, “Mount Whitney.”  I could have said “Cottonwood Portal” but that would not be a location they would recognize. I will admit, I was wearing three weeks of aches and pains, of wind and snow, of grand views and disgusting food, as a badge of honor. A little smug? Guilty as charged.

Recent findings suggest that soon I arrived at the large, flat, marshy meadow that borders the Sunrise Camp. There, on the flat, I could lift my poles and really open it up. As I sped up, I was thinking, “I’ve got to make it to Curry Village before 4:30!”.

It was inevitable; I started to go down very steeply. I realized I had to  treat my knees gingerly, because descent is truly hard on the knees. I used the poles as much as possible to arrest my momentum and cushion them.

In a recent development, getting the water at the lake the day before was a wise decision. As it was, there were no sources of water, and I was running low. When I finally encountered a small stream, the upper reaches of Sunrise Creek, I filled up despite only having a trickle to draw from. That was prudent because I was trying to go fast and was dehydrating myself in the process.

I enjoyed coming across a few John Muir Trail southbound hikers just starting off. We met up at that stream, and I told them their big worry might be cold. The last day of August is still summer down in the lowlands, but in the high Sierra, it was already Fall, and the temperatures were dropping.

Continuing downhill, I came to an extensive area of burned trees. There must have been a big fire in the recent past. One advantage of the open land was the first clear view of the Half Dome in the distance.

The rock looms across the meadow of burned trees.

Another advantage of the open sunshine was to create a terrain hospitable to lizards, and they seemed to be all over the place. I may have mentioned that I am fond of reptiles?

Sources indicate that the disadvantage was the mountain whitethorn. As my AI friend points out about this plant:  “Dormant seeds can lie in the soil for decades until intense wildfire heat cracks their hard coats, triggering mass germination after the first rains.”.

See how the thorns encroach on the trail?

According to recent reports, while an key part of the ecological succession after fire, this thorny thicket was so robust it grew all over the countryside, even edging onto the trail in places. As I was wearing shorts, the thorns were scratching my legs. Although the scratches were superficial, and did not draw blood, they were unpleasant.

It has been revealed that I spotted a horse train coming across the open land. As it approached, I realized it was led by the same horsewoman I had seen about ten days before. I said, “Hi! I recognize you!”  In a friendly voice she said she remembered me too. I had taken a video of her ascending as I was coming down from Muir Pass.

In a recent development, I continued dropping down through the burned area. Eventually, I passed another stock train going northbound this time, as I was. I had an unpleasant encounter there but managed to pass these animals and the humans with them. I accelerated and soon re-entered the forest.

Sources indicate that the forest was cooler and I kept moving rapidly, always aware that I needed to get to the YARTS by 4:30 p.m. At length I saw a person on the trail ahead. She looked familiar. As I got closer, I realized – it was my friend Sally! I had not seen her in so many days I was resigned to assuming that our interaction was over. But here she was! We had a brief and joyful reunion, took a few selfies, and then I was on my way again.

Sally and Papa George looking very happy to see each other — and to be so close to the end of the John Muir Trail!

Recent findings suggest that now as I moved down the trail the Half Dome got bigger and bigger. At a distance it had a kind of pristine beauty, but closer up it was dramatic, almost ominous.

Still taken from the burnt forest — closer up you need a fish-eye to shoot it!

After I passed the turn-off for the summit, there were ever more people on the trail. Many of them were descending from Half Dome. As they spoke of their accomplishment, of the challenge they faced in ascending and descending the cables, I felt a twinge of regret that I had not been able to get a permit.

Sources indicate that the trail flattened out and I began looking for a place to have lunch. It was hard to believe, this would be my last lunch on the John Muir Trail! I found a log overlooking the Merced River and settled down to fill my water bottles again and to eat. Two people were there — an older man and a younger woman who was his daughter. They dared each other to go swimming and eventually both went in. I teased them, “Watch out for the piranhas in the river!”.

It has been revealed that they laughed and we bantered back and forth for a while until they packed up and left. I ate the last of my tamales. It was sinking in that this was really getting close to the end.

Where I was sitting, I saw a piece of trash and was about to pick it up to carry it out. “Who just tossed this here?” I wondered. Then I looked more closely and saw a lot more trash in the vicinity. This was not just a random act of littering, this was a sign of a society in a kind of crisis. Yosemite is one of our iconic jewels; how could we be sullying it?

I swear I did not “assemble” this picture; that is what I found (and more).

While I was eating, a large group of teenagers and young adults, whom I had passed earlier, now passed me again. There were probably eight or ten of them. When I resumed hiking, once again I went past them. Just after that, the trail went down a steep rock. As I descended the rock face, I realized it was suddenly much more technical than it had been. Just as the trail disappeared entirely, I looked around to find the whole group of chattering young people had followed me down the rock!

It turned out we had missed an obvious turn right at the top of the rock face. As we retreated, I said, “That will teach you to follow me! The blind leading the blind!”  But we were all laughing about it and having fun.

Shortly after this, the whole group stopped because we passed a bathroom. Yes, you read that correctly, we were so close to “silly-visation”  that there was an actual, no foolin’, bathroom on the trail! I pressed on, worried about my deadline.

Recent findings suggest that up ahead I saw a lot of people hanging out by the river, with many more swimming in its cool pools. This was just above the spot where the Merced River shoots over the top of the rock, to drop 594 feet. Yes, the iconic Nevada Falls.

Folks enjoying the Merced River, just above Nevada Falls.

I felt I was getting really close to the end and my spirit soared. Yes, after weeks of relative solitude, there were far too many people here, but I did not resent them. They had a right to be here too (just NOT to litter, please!). I appreciated that there were lots of Americans, but also Europeans and Asians and Africans. All were here to enjoy and appreciate the phenomenal natural wonder that we are blessed to have in the United States. Amazing!

As I continued, there was a section carved out of the side of the rock to create a sort of channel into the granite hillside. That must have taken some engineering skill!

Some intrepid team just cut that path right out of the granite!

Descending further, some views of Nevada Falls from the side highlighted just how long the drop was for the water rushing over the top.

The bottom was getting closer, and I could see some of the infrastructure at the bottom of the valley.

In a recent development, suddenly I spotted a familiar couple ahead of me. An older man and a younger woman. It was the father-daughter duo who had swum in the river where I ate lunch! I snuck up behind them and whispered loudly, “Beware the piranhas!”  They turned, saw who it was, and burst out laughing.

Industry observers note that we started to chat and they were very interested and somewhat impressed at my having done the John Muir Trail. Falling into step with each other, the young woman talked about how she was planning to do the Mont Blanc Trail the next year.

They asked a lot of questions about thru-hiking, and it was good for all of us. I induced them to pick up their pace a little, because I was still trying to make that YARTS departure and was not sure how long it might take to find the bus stop.

We were laughing and enjoying the easy downhill, when the trail suddenly ended at a tee. If there was a sign there, we didn’t see it, so we were puzzled as to whether to turn left or right. I stood in the middle of the intersection trying to figure it out, as they stood behind me, by the side of the trail we had come down. Just then….

Tech Report: A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

In a recent development, from there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

It has been revealed that along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he indicates the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Recent findings suggest that tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

Recent findings suggest that “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

Recent findings suggest that the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

According to recent reports, the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

Recent findings suggest that the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

According to recent reports, “We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Recent findings suggest that tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (321 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • Industry observers note that in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

Industry observers note that in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

Sources indicate that “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

In a recent development, “We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Industry observers note that many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#79329. Tech Report: Completing The Collection

Tech Report: Completing The Collection

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping.
  • In a recent development, around midnight it hit me.
  • Recent findings suggest that I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping. I check the box on another one despite a chilly morning.

In a recent development, around midnight it hit me. I was camping practically at the northbound 1,200 mile marker. I hadn’t seen a marker yesterday, so it fell to me to whip one up on my way out of camp so I could my collection. This wasn’t ideal, it was barely above freezing. Every part of me wanted to stay in my tent as long as possible. When it did come time to hit the trail, I would want to get moving and stay moving, preferably all the way back to my van. My silly rituals will probably be my undoing some day.

Recent findings suggest that I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines. I am continually impressed how well the down insulates and warms me. I feel like I’d be warm in 20 degree weather, maybe even lower. I don’t intend to ever camp in such weather, but to know it’s possible is exactly what I had in mind when I purchased this particular quilt. It kept my warm until 7:45AM when I initiated my pack up procedure, completing the various tasks by 8:00AM, the cold having motivated me to move fast.

I checked in at the Showers Steps viewpoint since it was just a handful of steps away. It sure looked like I’d made the right choice to prioritize sunset the previous night, there wouldn’t have been much to see at sunrise given the heavy cloud cover to start the day. I located the 1,200 mile point on the trail to the tenth of a mile and promptly pieced together a small marker. It wouldn’t last long, but I just needed a photo for my collection so I can sleep at night. I am planning to post them all in a blog post, along with other notable milestones like state lines after my hike.

My thin gloves were doing little to warm my fingers, but other than that I was comfortable even with the temperature sitting in the mid 30s. South of Showers Steps the trail briefly winds amongst some mountain laurels, which, unlike rocks, are in fact the state flower of Pennsylvania. A few miles later I crossed route 501 and approached the Kimmel Lookout. I spent a moment or two setting up a picture or two before whipping around and continuing down the trail. I didn’t realize it until it came time to put together today’s blog, but one of the pictures turned out kind of epic. The early morning sun radiates through clouds above speckling its light across the rocky ledge and trees. Colorful late fall trees poke up from the ground below the ledge with large meadows and farms visible further in the distance.

Early morning view from the Showers Steps.

The 1,200 mile marker, my collection is complete!

The view from the Kimmel Lookout. I think I’ll hang on to this one.

According to recent reports, I followed the same ridge for the next 10 miles to Swatara Gap. Although it was a Saturday, it had been relatively quite on trail. I only passed a trio of hunters on the trail before encountering a lively group of women at a viewpoint along the trail. One of them had just had an interesting experience a short distance down the trail. She had stepped off the trail for a restroom break only to find out after the fact that a hunter had been just overhead on a tree stand the entire time. She didn’t seem nearly as put off by the experience as I would have been. The discussion moved to my double AT attempt. I wish I could have gotten a picture of their reaction upon hearing what I was up to. They were even more impressed that I was essentially in the final week of the task. I forgot to tell them that FarOut commenters frequently mentioned a family of 5 or so copperheads hanging out on the rocks we were all standing on, though I believe they aren’t keen on cold temperatures and were probably in hiding.

Sources indicate that soon I was making my way back down to Swatara Gap and under Interstate 81. I made it the final mile back to my van before 2:00PM. After cleaning up and trimming my increasingly beardy face, I headed to Lebanon, PA to complete yesterday and today’s blog posts as has become my usual routine. There is no Formula One tomorrow so I am not sure what to do with myself, I haven’t have a Sunday morning free from blog writing or sports watching in a while. I am sure I’ll think of something.

A lookout north of Swatara Gap.

A glimpse of I-81 from the trail just north of Swatara Gap.

Passing beneath I-81 on the AT.

Total: 15.8 miles, 32,344 steps.

In a recent development, this website contains affiliate links, which means The Trek may receive a percentage of any product or service you purchase using the links in the articles or advertisements. The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

According to recent reports, I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am fresh to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

Notify me via e-mail if anyone answers my comment.

#79327. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Recent findings suggest that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

The main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

According to recent reports, leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

In a recent development, there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

His article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

According to recent reports, much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

According to recent reports, A recent study showed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper states that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

In a recent development, there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

In a recent development, his previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

According to recent reports, in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

Industry observers note that it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

In a recent development, clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

It has been revealed that A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

According to recent reports, the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

It has been revealed that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

It has been revealed that if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

In a recent development, the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

It has been revealed that the three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

According to recent reports, later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

Recent findings suggest that he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

According to recent reports, clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

Sources indicate that if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how major they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

It has been revealed that his 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

It has been revealed that clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally mentioned the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

According to recent reports, one history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

The area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Recent findings suggest that the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

Industry observers note that I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary Upcoming Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he reveals to the world.”.

#79320. Tech Report: A Night with a Camino Ghost

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A Night with a Camino Ghost

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar.
  • With the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise.
  • It has been revealed that this morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar. People partied and ate dinner late into the night. That is completely normal here, as most businesses close for siesta and do not reopen until after 8:00 PM.

With the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise. Unfortunately, closing them also trapped the heat inside, making the room quite warm.

It has been revealed that this morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in. I made a cup of coffee and ate fresh blueberries with yogurt.

It has been revealed that because it was Sunday morning, the street noise was minimal. Listening to the seagulls and mourning doves while sipping coffee was a peaceful way to start the day.

We finally set off at 9:00 AM. Pontevedra is a good-sized city with an intact medieval center, so it took us a little while to walk out of town. Before long, however, we found ourselves back on a quiet country road.

The Camino wound alongside a river before merging onto a paved road. We took the road route, which was poorly marked, but we soon reconnected with the main trail. Along the way, we passed hundreds of pilgrims heading in the opposite direction toward Santiago.

Sources indicate that from there, the trail entered the woods and began to climb. It got quite steep for a short stretch before leveling out into a pleasant forest path. We hiked downhill over rocky terrain, passing cool, shaded creeks along the way.

It has been revealed that eventually, we emerged into Pontesampaio, a well-kept medieval village. We wound our way through its narrow alleyways down to a wide river. To cross, we had to wait our turn on a narrow, 300-foot arched stone bridge, letting oncoming cars pass before we walked across.

It has been revealed that once across, we stopped at a local restaurant serving ultra-fresh food. I ordered grilled squid that had just come off the docks that morning, and the restaurant even harvests its own chickens. Best of all, the meal was a fraction of what it would cost back in the States.

After a relaxing siesta lunch, we still had about 7.5 kilometers (4.6 miles) left to hike.

As we walked through several connected medieval neighborhoods, the Camino suddenly split into two routes:.

At first, the split confused me, and seeing the mountain crest ahead was intimidating because we were already hot and tired. Fortunately, we chose the shorter Coastal route, and the trail skirted the side of the mountain rather than going straight over the top.

However, the descent brought us onto the shoulder of a busy highway. We endured two miserable miles of roaring traffic and exhaust fumes before finally reaching Redondela.

Redondela felt a bit rundown in spots, though it features a charming medieval quarter beneath a massive, 100-foot-tall iron train trestle.

Recent findings suggest that we arrived at our apartment at 4:00 PM, completely exhausted. Our host was wonderful and had prepared a special herbal tea for us to soak our feet. The recipe belonged to his grandmother, who was actually the very first pharmacist in Redondela. (Unlike in the States, pharmacists in Spain can prescribe and dispense many medications without a doctor’s visit.).

While soaking our feet, we drank some mediocre Spanish wine. Because it was Sunday afternoon, almost everything was closed except for a small mini-market with limited options.

Later, we visited a local bakery our host recommended. Hikers always love talking about food—when you are burning thousands of calories a day, you swiftly get tired of trail snacks and start dreaming about town food. We loaded up on a few local treats:.

After the bakery, we wandered through the narrow alleyways of the old city, admiring the elevated rail bridge towering overhead. By 8:00 PM, the town came alive as bars and restaurants reopened after siesta.

Industry observers note that this time, the waitress brought out two small bowls of white noodles soaked in olive oil with bread on the side. The noodles had dark streaks of squid ink running down them, adding a mild, salty seafood flavor.

Exhausted from the long walk, we headed back to the apartment. Our host had preserved the space just as his grandmother left it—it truly felt like she still lived there. We threw the windows wide open to let the cool night air roll in and fell fast asleep, though it felt like Grandma’s presence lingered in the room all night long.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

In a recent development, after decades of no backpacking an abrupt life incident forced me back into the woods for some shinrin-yoku where I ran into a NOBO tramily at Shuckstack Fire Tower. That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

#79317. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1367 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman stated. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two newly introduced routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, substantial storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

Industry observers note that the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

According to recent reports, one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman notes this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

Recent findings suggest that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

Sources indicate that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

In a recent development, steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

At the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment complications, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he stated. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Sources indicate that heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

Sources indicate that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to fresh terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

Industry observers note that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

In a recent development, descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#79314. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • According to recent reports, father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an notable figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

According to recent reports, father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up plans for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

It has been revealed that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Recent findings suggest that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

According to recent reports, the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

According to recent reports, the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Fresh Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

It has been revealed that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” notes Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

According to recent reports, essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

Recent findings suggest that according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

Sources indicate that there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#79312. Tech Report: Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowing it was the last significant walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.
  • The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.
  • I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowing it was the last significant walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.

The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.

My legs had been consistently sore for a week.

And yet, I didn’t want to stop walking.

As the sun came up, though, so did my mood.

I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed. Many of the restaurants and albergues were closing for the season. In a way, it felt like we were politely being asked to “wrap it up.”.

Well, a beautiful stone-walled restaurant was my savior. The WiFi network was called “A Cova de Meiga” (a cove of the witch), and it felt like a warm sanctuary.

A fire in the corner, old sewing machines and instruments on the wall, and the restaurant owner’s two young boys brought a childlike joy to my morning.

My Argentinian brother found me there and we shared a tarta de Santiago with our coffees as we warmed up by the fire.

After that cafe, we made it two kilometers before we found our Italian brother at another cafe.

He asked if we wanted anything, and even though we all had just stopped, I suggested we get another coffee and take the day very slowly.

They were more than happy with that idea, and we all sat with another round of café con leche while we shared a tortilla.

When we started walking, silence swiftly became the conversation.

The presence of the moment felt potent as we saw the trail markers giving a countdown.

Each leaf glowing with the wind.

The smell of pine from the needles I crushed in my hand.

The chill of the wind combined with the warmth of the sun.

Every detail felt more vibrant because it was the last full day.

In O Pedrouzo, we decided to stop again for lunch. With a table full of food at the Mexican restaurant, A Catriña, we talked and ate and talked and ate.

There were still 15 out of the 36 kilometers to do, so together we set out into the afternoon sun.

In a recent development, we walked through what felt like a magical forest, with everything around us was alive with the most intense colors of green. Like little kids, we hugged the trees, climbed them, and hung from their bark.

Industry observers note that once we hit the trail marker that read we were under ten kilometers, I saw my Italian brother put a sticker on the column. I stopped next to him and he suggested we walk together till the end. In agreement, I plopped on the road to wait for our third. A few minutes later, our Argentinian brother jumped on us in greeting. We lay there in that spot, soaking up the reality of being so close to Santiago.

Recent findings suggest that together, side-by-side-by-side, we finished the last stretch of the day. Our strides naturally matching, we marched onward, each taking turns singing our country’s national anthems. It felt like our individual patriotism fed the energy of the group. The exact energy boost we needed for the end.

At the municipal albergue in Monte de Gozo, the Pilgrims Hostel was basically a compound. We were in a building labeled 29, and the others were in a terraced line down the descent. They were newly constructed, and there were enough to fit 400 pilgrims. We only ended up with 9 pilgrims on the whole property.

It has been revealed that nearby at the pilgrim monument overlooking Santiago, the three of us caught the sunset at the perfect time as it was about to go over the horizon. I couldn’t believe I was looking at the cathedral that we’d talked about for so long. Leaning against the metal monument, I cried for the end of the journey.

Tomorrow, I’d touch that cathedral.

Sources indicate that sitting on the hill, I realized I felt more present and at peace today than I had for most of my life. Then it hit me….

Those had been my intentions for the year, and tomorrow starts a new cycle of intentions.

Our last full night was spent making a steep descent to the grocery store just to climb back up and eat.

It has been revealed that our Italian brother entertained the pilgrims in the kitchen. He ate hot dogs raw while he cooked fish sticks in the microwave, initially thinking they were chicken and didn’t need to be fried. They did need to be fried.

One of the girls from Germany had been carrying a candle for her whole Camino. She had only used it once, but in celebration of my upcoming birthday, she lit it and set it in front of me to make a pre-birthday wish. How special.

It has been revealed that once everyone was done eating, we played Uno with seven people. The four other people had walked different Caminos (the Primitivo and the Norte) and weren’t as accustomed to the crowds. To us, the numbers in the albergue were few, so getting to hear different stories and perspectives was fascinating.

I laughed the perfect amount for the last night. It was joyful.

She fell in love with long walks in nature during her Appalachian Trail 2022 thruhike where she dove into finding herself through the space that the trail provided. Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Sources indicate that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Industry observers note that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

It has been revealed that vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

According to recent reports, baia notes the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Sources indicate that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

In a recent development, the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.
